title: Simon Says
intro: Watch the pattern of lights and sounds, then copy it. It gets longer every round.

wiring_steps.title: The red light and button
wiring_steps.text: Unplug the USB cable before you change any wires. Plug it back in when you're done. Start with the power rails: a black wire from GND on your board to the blue (−) rail at the bottom of the breadboard, and a red wire from {{VCC}} to the red (+) rail. Push the red LED into holes H2 and H3, with the long leg (+) in H3. Put a 220Ω resistor from G2 across the gap to E2. Add a wire from {{pin:LED_RED}} to J3, and a black wire from A2 to the blue (−) rail at the bottom. Press the red button into the middle of the breadboard so it sits across the gap: its legs go in F5, F7, E5 and E7. Add a wire from {{pin:BUTTON_RED}} to J5, and a black wire from A7 to the blue (−) rail. (The code turns on the pin's pull-up, so no resistor is needed.)

wiring_steps.title: The yellow light and button
wiring_steps.text: Push the yellow LED into holes H9 and H10, with the long leg (+) in H10. Put a 220Ω resistor from G9 across the gap to E9. Add a wire from {{pin:LED_YELLOW}} to J10, and a black wire from A9 to the blue (−) rail at the bottom. Press the yellow button into the middle of the breadboard so it sits across the gap: its legs go in F12, F14, E12 and E14. Add a wire from {{pin:BUTTON_YELLOW}} to J12, and a black wire from A14 to the blue (−) rail. (The code turns on the pin's pull-up, so no resistor is needed.)

wiring_steps.title: The buzzer
wiring_steps.text: The buzzer sits beside the breadboard. Connect its + leg (the red wire, or the leg marked +) to {{pin:BUZZER_PIN}}, and its − leg (the black wire) to the blue (−) rail.

steps.title: Lights and notes
steps.text:
Four colours, each with its own light and note. Instead of writing everything four times, we keep the pins and notes in **arrays**: numbered lists. `LEDS[0]` is the first one (red), `LEDS[3]` the last (blue).

The `flash(colour)` function lights one colour and plays its note.

**Your task:** Run it. Then change the notes to make your own tune.
hints: Change the numbers in `NOTES` and Run again.

checks.label: All four lights flash, each with a note

steps.success: Four colours, one function. That's the power of arrays.

steps.title: Press a colour
steps.text:
Now each button flashes its own colour. One `for` loop checks all four buttons.

**Your task:** fill in the blanks.
hints: Use the array of buttons, with `i` to choose which one.
Flash the same colour number as the button.

checks.label: Each button flashes its own colour

steps.success: Every button works, with one loop.

steps.title: Simon Says
steps.text: **Goal:** the full game. Each round, Simon adds a random colour to the pattern and plays the whole pattern. You copy it with the buttons. Get it right and the next round starts (print `Round 2`, `Round 3`...). Get it wrong and it's game over.
hints: Keep the pattern in an array (`int pattern[100];`) and how long it is in `length`.
A function that waits for any button and returns which colour was pressed makes copying easy.
Use **Watch the goal**, then build it one function at a time.
steps.success: Simon Says! Your game remembers a growing list, just like you do.

outro: You built Simon Says with **arrays**: lists of pins, notes and the growing pattern. Arrays and **for loops** let one piece of code handle all four colours.
stretch: Make it speed up as the pattern gets longer.
Keep a high score and print it after each game.
Play a victory tune after every 5 rounds.
